title: openSoom — the ventilation decision, from start to finish

lines: A running fan sounds reassuring. In this food production zone, the airflow tells a different story.
OpenSoom follows one ventilation decision, from the first observation through to the result a manager can verify.
A Korean performance assessment covered three hundred and one schools after their kitchens had received ventilation improvements.
In that group, seventeen point nine percent still received an inadequate rating. That finding raises a practical question.
Once equipment is operating, how do you check the result in each zone?
This is the actual openSoom dashboard, connected to a running oneM2M service. Its sensors and actuators are simulated.
The cooking line, wash station and packing area each have their own profile. Selecting the cooking line brings up the measurements behind its alert.
The fan reports that it is running. Airflow is three hundred and sixty cubic metres per hour. This zone calls for nine hundred.
From the zone inspection, the operator requests a fully open damper. The service checks the facility, permission and freshness of the observation.
The device acknowledges the command. OpenSoom waits for two fresh observations after that acknowledgement.
On this run the airflow reaches one thousand and thirty five, and the incident can close.
A second supplier should be able to join without rewriting the dashboard. Here is a recorded example of what oneM2M contributes.
A device creates an observation over MQTT with TLS. A management application retrieves the same resource over HTTPS.
Both responses carry the same resource identifier. The standard platform connects the two protocols.
At the second facility, the same dashboard opens a learning studio, a meeting room and a shared lounge.
This supplier reports airflow in litres per second. The adapter converts it into cubic metres per hour before the operating tools read it.
The studio is at two hundred against its own five hundred target. The operator requests the same damper action.
In this run the damper acknowledges the request and reaches one hundred percent. The next observations still show only two hundred.
The service keeps the incident open. A maintenance technician can inspect the equipment with the command, acknowledgement and later measurements together.
These two runs demonstrate how the same operating procedure produces different, traceable decisions.
We also tested a separate deployment with an operations application and a maintenance application running as independent processes.
Each has its own oneM2M application identity and subscription. A device publishes one abnormal observation. Both applications receive a notification and retrieve the underlying resource.
Operations checks the zone and requests a permitted action. Maintenance uses the same event identifier to create a work order for inspection.
The service platform handles delivery and access control. The two applications own different decisions.
These records come from that separate software run. The event identifier connects the original observation to both outputs.
The operations report records what happened to the command. The maintenance work order gives inspection staff a traceable reason to investigate.
A recorded airflow recovery cannot certify that a technician inspected the equipment. The work order remains a separate responsibility.
A different role should not silently inherit equipment control. The separate applications test includes an attempted command from maintenance.
The oneM2M platform denies the write. Separate role tests also block an observer reading another facility.
The demonstration runs locally. A deployment in a working facility would also need site authentication and commissioning.
A manager can also use an agent. The Codex plugin and a standalone model runner share the same operating tools.
Here a hosted model discovered resources, read a group, examined evidence, requested an action and checked the result twice.
The first check was still waiting. The second found the required observations. The server retained the run independently of the model's written answer.
In a separate recorded experiment, a central service connected two local facilities. We interrupted the central service for just over fourteen seconds.
The food facility continued its local command, acknowledgement and recovery check. When the connection returned, the service rejected an expired request.
The local facility kept the same serving platform throughout this experiment.
The repository includes both facility profiles, the two supplier adapters, and a deterministic demonstration that runs without an AI account.
A maintainer installs the local service and checks readiness. A manager can then inspect the facility from the dashboard or through the Codex plugin.
To adapt another site, configure its zones and targets, map the supplier units, and validate observations before enabling any physical control.
OpenSoom gives facilities a shared way to ask what changed after ventilation equipment acted.
Explore the code, replay the scenarios and inspect the underlying evidence in the openSoom repository.
